An ecologist is a scientist who studies the relationships between living things and the world around them.

That one sentence is the heart of it. But to truly understand what it means, you need to unpack three things: who an ecologist is, what they study, and why it matters.
Understanding the Word from the Inside Out

Before understanding what an ecologist is, you need to briefly understand what ecology is, because an ecologist is simply a person who practises ecology.

Ecology is the branch of science that asks: "How do living things relate to each other and to their surroundings?"

Notice that ecology is not just about animals or plants in isolation. It is about relationships — the invisible threads that connect a bee to a flower, a wolf to a deer, a tree to the soil, and rainfall to a whole forest. An ecologist's entire job is to find, study, and understand those threads.

An ecologist goes out into the world — forests, oceans, deserts, wetlands, cities — and asks questions like:

  • Why do certain animals live in this place but not that one?
  • What happens to a river ecosystem if one species of fish disappears?
  • How does a rise in temperature affect the plants in a meadow?
  • Why are the populations of certain birds declining?
  • How do nutrients flow from the soil into plants, then into animals, and back again?

To answer these questions, an ecologist observes, measures, records, and analyses. They count animal populations. They test soil and water. They track the movement of species. They build models to predict what might happen if conditions change. It is a deeply scientific process — data-driven, careful, and methodical.
The Scale of What an Ecologist Studies

One of the most fascinating things about ecology — and therefore about ecologists — is that they can zoom in or zoom out dramatically in what they study. Think of it like a camera lens:

Zoomed all the way in — an ecologist might study the relationship between a single species of insect and the specific plant it feeds on.

In the middle — an ecologist might study a whole community of animals and plants in a particular pond or woodland, and how they all affect each other.

Zoomed all the way out — an ecologist might study an entire ecosystem (such as the Amazon rainforest or the Arctic tundra) and how energy, water, carbon, and life all cycle through it at a massive scale.

This range of scale is unique to ecology. Not many sciences stretch so comfortably from the tiny to the enormous.

Because the living world is so vast, ecologists often specialise. Here are the main kinds:

Marine ecologists study relationships in oceans and seas — coral reefs, deep-sea creatures, coastal habitats.

Terrestrial ecologists focus on land-based ecosystems — forests, grasslands, deserts, mountains.

Freshwater ecologists study lakes, rivers, ponds, and streams.

Wildlife ecologists focus specifically on animal populations — their behaviour, movement, survival, and interaction with their habitat.

Plant ecologists (sometimes called vegetation ecologists) study how plants interact with each other and their environment.

Microbial ecologists study the ecology of microscopic organisms like bacteria and fungi, which play enormous roles in ecosystems even though we cannot see them.

Conservation ecologists apply ecological knowledge specifically to protect endangered species and disappearing habitats.

Urban ecologists study how nature functions within cities and human-dominated landscapes — pigeons on rooftops, foxes in suburbs, insects in city parks.

All of these people are ecologists. The label changes based on what part of the living world they focus on, but the core job — studying relationships between living things and their environment — remains the same.
What Makes an Ecologist Different from Similar Roles?

It is easy to confuse an ecologist with other related roles. Here is how to tell them apart:

An ecologist vs. a biologist — A biologist is a broad term for anyone who studies living things. An ecologist is a specific type of biologist whose focus is always on relationships and environments, not just on organisms themselves.

An ecologist vs. an environmentalist — An environmentalist is someone who advocates for protecting the environment, often through activism, policy, or public campaigning. An ecologist is a scientist — their primary role is to study and understand nature, not necessarily to campaign for it. That said, many ecologists are also passionate environmentalists, and their scientific findings often fuel environmental campaigns.

An ecologist vs. a zoologist or botanist — A zoologist studies animals; a botanist studies plants. An ecologist studies the relationships between living things (which may include animals and plants), and between those living things and their physical environment (soil, water, climate, etc.).

The work of ecologists is arguably more important today than at any point in history. Here is why:

Every major environmental crisis humanity faces — climate change, species extinction, deforestation, ocean dead zones, shrinking biodiversity — is fundamentally an ecological problem. These are crises of broken or disrupted relationships in living systems.

Ecologists are the scientists who can actually diagnose what is going wrong. They tell us: "If we remove this species, the whole system collapses." Or: "If the temperature rises by two degrees, these forests will no longer be able to sustain themselves." Or: "This seemingly empty patch of land is actually a critical breeding ground for three endangered species."

Without ecologists, we would be making decisions about the natural world in the dark. With them, we have a fighting chance to understand what we are damaging and how to restore it.

An ecologist is a scientist who studies how living things — plants, animals, microbes, and humans — relate to each other and to their physical environment (soil, water, air, climate). They work at many scales, from small ponds to entire continents, and often specialise in particular environments like oceans, forests, or cities. Their work is essential for understanding, protecting, and restoring the natural world.
